subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DAIRY POLICY FOR YEAR COMMENCING APRIL 1, 1971

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DAIRY POLICY FOR YEAR COMMENCING APRIL 1, 1971
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement with respect to dairy policy for the year starting April 1, 1971. The Canadian Dairy Commission has been authorized to pay subsidy on manufacturing milk and cream, under its quota system, at the same rate as in the year just ending. This is $1.25 per 100 pounds of milk testing 3.5 per cent butterfat, or 35.71 cents per pound of butterfat.
The prices at which the commission offers to purchase major dairy products in support of Canadian prices will, for the present, remain at existing levels. It will be recalled that the prices for skim milk powder and Cheddar cheese were each advanced four cents per pound on February 8 last, bringing the present rates to 24 cents per pound for powder and 51 cents for cheese. The butter support price continues at 65 cents per pound.
While actual prices received by producers from the market are a matter of provincial jurisdiction, these changes will mean that in the forthcoming dairy year there will be a significant increase in market prices to producers for industrial milk compared with those in effect at the start of this dairy year. There is a holdback from payments to producers toward the cost of disposing of surplus dairy products which have to be exported.
There was a change in this procedure during the past year with the adoption in Ontario and Quebec of a system of market-sharing quotas for all producers supplying milk for manufacturing use. With that change the Commission paid producers in those provinces the full rate of subsidy and a levy was made from the market payment and remitted to the commission.
This arrangement will continue during the coming year. In provinces where producers are now under market-sharing quotas, or at any time during the year when other provinces may come under the system, producers will receive subsidy at the full rate for the quantity of milk or cream for which they are eligible. This, of course, is conditional on a levy being taken from the market payment by the provincial board and remitted to the commission. In provinces not under market-sharing quotas there will continue to be a levy or holdback from the subsidy payments.
The major surplus Canadian dairy product is skim milk powder. The cost of disposing of surpluses, and the rate of levy necessary to finance that cost, is related primarily to the price which can be secured for skim milk powder exports.
Starting a year ago there has been a marked improvement in that price from the levels which prevailed previously. It is difficult for the commission at this time to estimate the price which will prevail for skim milk powder exports during the coming year and, in consequence, its costs of disposing of surpluses and the rate of levy from producer payments necessary to finance them.
It will be at least a month, and probably more, before this situation is clarified.
In the meantime, the rates of levy or holdback from producer payments will, with one exception, continue at present levels. The only change, for the present, is that the levy of 1 cent per pound of butterfat on cream

deliveries by a producer up to his quota will be discontinued.
The commission, however, may later adjust these rates when it is better able to estimate its costs of surplus disposal for the coming year.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DAIRY POLICY FOR YEAR COMMENCING APRIL 1, 1971
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the minister for providing me with a copy of this announcement well before the House opened. Those dairy producers who have been holding their collective breath waiting for this announcement may now let their breath out slowly because there will not be much of a change as a result of this announcement. Certainly there will be no help to counteract the increased costs which they are experiencing every year.
It is evident that there has never been as much dissatisfaction among dairy farmers in this country as there is at the present time. A few years back we had overproduction in Canada. Now production in relation to needs is just about holding its own in all provinces outside of Ontario and Quebec, or central Canada. We may soon be depending on imports. Have the powers that be no knowledge of how long it takes to establish a dairy business and the cost involved? The farmers may well end up in a position of deficit production shortly. It is evident that the prime object seems to be to get the government out of paying subsidies, with sufficient production only a secondary aim.
The past year has shown an increase in the disappearance of dairy surpluses in North America and western Europe. This tendency to decline began about the middle of 1969. Prices are therefore strengthening. There has also been a general decline in the number of dairy cows as well as in the number of producers. The average production per cow is up which shows increased efficiency in production. This is something the government is always talking about, especially the Department of Agriculture.
Since the Canadian Dairy Commission began operating in 1967 the number of registered producers has dropped by approximately 50 per cent. This means that the other half is no longer in business. Half of the former producers no longer have an income from the dairy business.
If the government insists on cheap food, subsidies must be paid. In fact, they may have to be increased; yet the government estimates a decrease for sustaining the dairy industry in the future.
In the recent agreement between Quebec and Ontario and the Canadian Dairy Commission fines were imposed-there is no other word for these holdbacks-of $2.40 per hundred on manufacturing milk for overproduction and 50.28 cents per pound of butterfat. The same deal is now proposed for Alberta. I understand that two or more preliminary meetings have been held in Alberta in this regard. Under this agreement the Canadian Dairy Commission can fine even fluid milk shippers for then-surplus or overproduction. With this type of agreement there is no way their surplus production can be reached by the Canadian Dairy Commission. These fines can put a producer in a straitjacket. He must hold his production to a certain level at all times. Anyone knows that cows refuse to co-operate, thus making this almost impossible.

Dairy farmers must wonder why their industry has been singled out to be the only Canadian industry under complete state control.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DAIRY POLICY FOR YEAR COMMENCING APRIL 1, 1971
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in effect the statement says there will be no change in the direction of dairy policy. That policy is mainly one by which the government is withdrawing support for the industry or reducing it to the minimum. I think this policy will fit in very well with the farm adjustment policy being worked out by the minister and his colleagues which seeks to remove an increasing number of farmers from agriculture. This adjustment program will adjust a number of farmers out of agriculture. I believe the dairy policy will fit into this program very well, to the dissatisfaction of the farmers. It is said that the dairy program will depend on what the export price is for powdered milk, which is an unknown factor.
The last time the minister made an announcement on dairy policy he said that an agreement had been reached between the dairy producers in Quebec and Ontario. Not more than two weeks later we had an urgent plea from the dairy producers in Quebec to appear before the Standing Committee on Agriculture to state their case and their dissatisfaction. At that time I asked them how they could expect the committee to do for them what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) had already refused to do.
This is the situation in which we find ourselves. I would not be surprised if we again have the dairy producers asking to appear before the Standing Committee on Agriculture as a result of this statement.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DAIRY POLICY FOR YEAR COMMENCING APRIL 1, 1971
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as it happens, I had planned to put a question related to the dairy policy to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson). I would have done so yesterday, but as he was absent and the new dairy year is fast drawing near I had hoped that he would inform us today of the new dairy policy for 1971-72.
Hon. members will remember that on February 17, 1971, the House instructed the Committee on Agriculture to inquire into Vote No. 30 related to the Canadian Dairy Commission and to report in due course to the House. As the Committee on Agriculture has unfortunately not examined this vote so far, I quite understand why today the Minister of Agriculture has announced no major changes in dairy policy for the coming year.
I expected, however, that the increase in production costs for dairy products as well as other products, would have been taken into account, and that some improvements would have been made that would have been more beneficial to those who are really involved in milk production, especially industrial milk, so that they could obtain a higher income and fairer prices.
Obviously, I am aware of the current difficulties of the Canadian government; I realize also that it is not always an easy task to accept the most legitimate requests from farm organizations, such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. But one should well understand that it will
March 30, 1971

Request for Seal Hunt Study
be necessary at some point to react more favourably if we are to establish a dairy industry that will be in a position to compete with products from elsewhere.
The minister is certainly aware that member countries of the European Common Market voted recently on the adoption of a budget of over $3 billion to subsidize the production of farm products, in order to allow producers to produce more efficiently and at lower cost.
If Canada is to remain on the international market, it will have some day to adopt policies to foster a decrease in production costs while enabling producers to earn a living decently.
Furthermore, a surplus is said to exist. Yes surely, there is a surplus, if the objective is set according to present consumer demand. It is obvious that the people's purchasing power is rapidly decreasing month after month as the rate of unemployment is increasing. There is no doubt then that demand in decreasing gradually. It is clear that the people would need a national market on which to dispose of a greater production, if it had a purchasing power to match its actual needs.
Then, there have been proposals during the past couple of years to the effect that by means of agreements the federal and provincial governments could generate a policy to help dispose of a given volume of dairy products in schools, hospitals, homes for senior citizens, etc.
This policy is presently established in the United States and in quite a forceful manner, as the President of the United States has just authorized doubling this year's budget to supply dairy products in schools, hospitals and homes.
This has promoted the consumption on the national market, and allowed United States milk producers to dispose more easily of their production and to have more profitable farms.
I repeat that the minister, his advisers and the government should further study these suggestions in order to find the means of carrying out this objective of helping the dairy industry of Canada, especially in the provinces with the higher volume, to continue its progress and establish research facilities towards diversification of its production for greater use of milk.
In any event, I offer the minister my co-operation and that of my colleagues so that we may continue to work together in order to find solutions that will ensure the survival of the milk producers because many of them have now gone bankrupt.
During the weekend, I witnessed typical cases which are really touching. As a matter of fact, I met people who had made capital expenditures to remain in the dairy industry and who, due to the increase of quota costs, are today under the obligation of recapitalizing or going bankrupt.
Therefore, I should like to invite the minister not to wait for the next dairy year to announce again an increase in the prices of industrial milk, but to do it, as is mentioned in the statement, within the limit of a month or two, which is what we hope for.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to move a motion pursuant to Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. It concerns the appointment of a government task force to investigate and study all aspects of the seal industry in Canadian waters, particularly the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Labrador waters, with a view to reducing the annual seal quota. The terms of reference contain no reference to the value of the seal hunt to the citizens of the Maritimes, Newfoundland and the Gaspe as a source of income and employment. The task force includes no member from those areas. The recommendations to be made by the task force are conditioned by the statement by the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) that it may be necessary to launch a campaign to have "the ladies stop buying fur seal coats."
I therefore move, with the consent of the House, seconded by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall):
That this House instructs the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry to inquire into the necessity for the appointment by the government of a task force to inquire into the seal industry in the Atlantic region and, in particular, to inquire into the rationale of having the task force composed entirely of persons from other than the Atlantic area.

Subclause (1) of clause 27 is on pages 9, 10 and the top half of page 11. This subclause provides for early retirement in the public service. It seems to be divided into four main categories. One could easily get lost in the detail, so all I shall do at this point is identify the four main categories as I see them.
First, there is a provision for public servants 55 years of age or over who have 30 or more years of public service. Second, there is a category of public servants 50 years of age or over who have 25 years or more of public service. The third category relates to those 55 years of age or over who have ten years or more of public service and are called upon to retire from the public service involuntarily. The fourth category consists of employees 50 years of age or over who have 20 years or more of public service. It might be said that there is a fifth category, but it is really a variation of one of the others.
There are differing formulas that apply to these various categories and, of course, there is a certain amount of overlapping, but if I may I shall move on to the main reason for my intervention in the debate at this time. Since we are in committee of the whole, it is likely that some of us may speak more than once. The idea of providing for early retirement, particularly when it is on a voluntary basis, is good and is highly welcomed. I knew that would bring a smile to the face of the hon. member for Ottawa West. The provis'on is that if a person is 55 years of age or over and has 30 years or more of service, he can retire and immediately draw a pension. The pension will be the amount that he has earned for that number of years service. Thirty years service at 2 per cent per year will give him a 60 per cent pension, namely 60 per cent of his average salary for his six best years. He will get
24081-19J
Government Organization Act, 1970
that full pension at that time without any reduction. Unless the man is to be put in the Senate there is not much more that can be done for him, and I would not wish that on my best friend in the Public Service.
I would go further, Mr. Chairman, and say that there are good things which can be said for the formulas which apply to the other categories when a public servant, of his own volition, wants to retire. The key element in all the other formulas, of course, is a reduction provision. Thus, if one is 50 years of age and has 25 years of service he can retire but his pension will not be 25 times 2 or in other words a 50 per cent pension; it will be reduced depending on how much he is short of age 55 or how much short he is of 30 years service. So, without going into detail, the same principle applies to the other categories I outlined. In other words, for all these people who do not meet the prime requirement of being 55 years of age and having 30 years service, early retirement has attached to it a provision whereby the pension one would draw would be reduced. If this were merely a voluntary scheme under which a public servant knowing the facts could choose to retire or, if he wished, choose to work to age 55 or 60, it would be hard to make a very strong case against it.
However, when one realizes that people in these categories may be involuntarily retired or, in effect, fired and placed on a pension at a reduced rate, this brings about a situation which prompts me to use a word I used when I spoke on this matter during second reading. I think it is ugly. I plead as strongly as I can with the President of the Treasury Board, who not only is the pilot of this legislation as a whole but also the pilot of this particular part, to reconsider this aspect of the matter. I plead with him not to try to sell us the line about it being a two-way street and that if it is fair one way it is. fair the other. It is the type of 50-50 arrangement involving one horse and one rabbit. To say it is all right for one public servant to have the choice of retiring on an early pension does not make it right for the big employer, the Federal Government, to force retirement on another individual when that forced retirement means a reduced pension.
People in the age bracket 50 to 55 are people who are trying to get their private affairs sorted out, get the mortgage as well as a few other things paid off and perhaps trying to get their sons and daughters through university. Their plans are made and they are looking toward retirement at age 60 or age 65. All of a sudden, the whole situation changes and instead of getting the pension they had hoped to get at age 60 or 65 they must take a greatly reduced pension. I plead on all the grounds I can muster that this is an unfair way for the government to treat its public servants. I ask the minister to-revise his thinking about it. I know it will be said that the government is a good employer and would not do some of these mean things; it would not fire people; it would not take advantage of this legislation. I am afraid I do not have that confidence, and I do not see how anyone in this House, no matter on which side he sits, could have that confidence.

Government Organization Act, 1970
We can recall a situation a year ago when people were retired when these pensions were not available to them. These were people who did not wish to leave the government service. But the government made some changes, and it will do so again. These changes could involve the desire to accommodate one language group here and another language group there and, perchance, there might be a desire to accommodate women in some positions in which they do not have adequate numbers and accommodate men in other positions in which they do not have sufficient numbers. There are all sorts of possibilities, under the government's policy, for public servants to be retired compulsorily. I suppose the government feels it will be able to say times have changed and that people previously had been retired with no pension, indeed had either to take their money out or receive a deferred pension at age 60. The government might say that now they will receive an immediate pension. However, the pension is subject to formulas which are spelled out in the different parts of new sub-section (1) of clause 27 of this bill.
As I say, early retirement is a good idea. I am glad the government is bringing it forward. I am glad it is provided in some other pieces of legislation. I think the man on the street is right when he says it would contribute to the solving of the unemployment problem, particularly of youth for people to retire earlier. I should like to see the old age pension age dropped from 65 to 60. But in view of the rights of people let us keep the voluntary principle alive. Let us not force people to take these reduced pensions because the government has put itself in the position of saying it is not putting people out on the street since it is giving them a pension.
When I spoke on this matter on second reading I gave an example. I notice the Letter Carriers Union of Canada has issued a press release today in which it highlights just about the same kind of example. Let me repeat it from memory. A person who is 50 years of age and has 20 years of public service can retire or be retired on an immediate pension. But under the formula by which he is retiring at age 50 his 20 years of service is ten years short of the 30 years he must have to retire at this point and, therefore, if you multiply ten by 5 it comes to 50 and his pension is reduced by 50 per cent. I see the President of the Treasury Bord giving me the courtesy of indicating that I am doing my arithmetic correctly, whether or not he agrees with my philosophy. So, let us consider a public servant who has given 20 years of service and who may retire or be forcibly retired He may think that with 20 years service he has built up a 40 per cent pension, 20 times two; but no, he has a pension which is reduced by 50 per cent and therefore at that age it is only 20 per cent of the average of his salary for the six best years. I hope no one stands up and says this is being nice to public servants and that it is something which they have not had before.
I say this is ugly and is something that will hang like a sword. I shall not say a Damoclesian sword because in the Hansard office last night we had difficulty spelling that word.

speechtext:
Thank you. I think this is the first time I ever publicly received this kind of service from the Chair. Thank you, Sir.
When we passed Bill C-194 in the last sess'on and provided for the escalation of pensions after retirement- a very good bill except for something that was in it, but I shall not reopen that at this point-we provided that those escalation payments could come into effect only at the age of 60 because that was the normal age for the retirement of public servants. In particular, the bill provided that retired RCMP or retired armed forces personnel who were under 60 could not get the increase right away but would have to wait until age 60. The main argument carried some weight, and the minister can find from the words in Hansard that I accepted his argument.
In committee we had a heated exchange of opinions but the committee was in too big a hurry to get the bill through, for reasons I need not mention. The main argument was that 60 was the minimum age at which public servants retired, except those who went out because of a medical disability, and therefore members of the RCMP or the armed forces who retired at an earlier age would have to wait. I now understand that when you combine the provisions of the bill now before us, specifically clause 27 of Bill C-207, with the provisions of the escalation legislation of a year ago, it turns out that when a public servant retires under this legislation at 55, 56, 52 or 53, he will qualify immediately for this 2 per cent escalation. I am glad of this, for I think it would be most unfortunate if these people being retired early did not get that benefit.
I ask the President of the Treasury Board whether that has not taken away completely his argument that he cannot provide this escalated pension for the retired armed forces and retired RCMP personnel because the normal retirement age is 60 and no one gets it under 60. Incidentally, members of Parliament who are out on pension and are under 60 do not get it either. But I am concerned at this point with the two groups I named. I say that if we are now revising that concept, if we are making it possible for the 2 per cent escalation to come into effect in the case of some public servants-there probably will be thousands of them-there is no justifica-
March 30, 1971

tion lor continuing that prohibition in the case ol retired members of the armed forces and retired members of the RCMP.
There is more that I want to say and more that I shall say, but we are in committee of the whole so one can speak aga'n. But in my view the main evil in this clause is the way in which pensions of people who retire early can be reduced, even when those people are retired against their will. I think that the bill should be amended to take care of that. Therefore, I move:
That clause 27 of Bill C-207 be amended by inserting therein, immediately following line 16 on page 11, as a conclusion to subparagraph (ii) of paragraph (c) of subsection (1) of section 11 of the Public Service Superannuation Act, the following words:
"provided however that the reductions indicated in this subparagraph shall not be applied in the case of any employee who does not retire voluntarily from the Public Service;"
I have already pointed out to the Chair that subclause (1) of clause 27 runs through pages 9, 10 and a half of page 11, and the place where I suggest these words should be added is in the middle of page 11, at the end of that subclause.
The reason I used the language "who does not retire voluntarily from the Public Service" is that the phrase is already in the clause with respect to one particular group. But I trust the whole point of my argument is clear that in the case of any public servant covered in any of the various parts of clause 27, who is retired against his will, there should be no reduction in the amount of the pension that he would get for the number of years that he has been employed in the public service.
As I said, there is much to be said about this legislation. I repeat without hesitation that in so far as it is voluntary, it is good. I repeat without hesitation that what it does for those 55 years of age and over with 30 years of service is excellent; I make no complaint about it. But surely we in this chamber do not want to put on the statute books a piece of legislation that makes it possible for the government to fire people between the ages of 50 to 55 and force them to take a reduced pension. That is the reason I have presented the amendment which I have the honour to move.

speechtext: I rise for the purpose of clarification, Mr. Chairman. While the hon. gentleman is correct that these payments are made out of a particular appropriation, there is no fund as such out of which these moneys are paid. He knows there is no such fund; he has made the point himself. They are paid out of an account which is made up of contributions at fixed rates made by employees, and a balancing or a residue comes from the public treasury or the Consolidated Revenue Fund. All payments into and out of the superannuation account are made from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and consequently any change in these payments is a direct charge on the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

Mr. Chairman, as the President of the Treasury Board will confirm, when I spoke earlier I did not use the word "fund". I used the word "account". I have been through this, around it and over it many times. I think we know what we are talking about. But I submit, Sir, that no additional appropriation, no voting of any money, not even a dollar, now or later, will be required by Parliament if this amendment carries.
The minister says there is no fund. No, there is not a separate bank account somewhere. But the same minister and the same government say the fact that that account is there by legislation means it is as good as gold, if gold is any good. And I submit, Sir, that the test of this is whether or not a subsequent appropriation, a subsequent estimate, a subsequent vote by Parliament would be necessary; and it would not be necessary, not at all. These pensions are paid out of the superannuation account without any specific vote by Parliament at all. I submit, on that test, Parliament is not being asked to vote additional money, and that Your Honour was right the first time.

If, as he suggests, his amendment would have the effect of conferring added security, added benefits on the employee at no cost to the consolidated revenue fund, I would be supporting it wholeheartedly. The fact of the matter is that this represents an additional cost, an increase in the contingent liability and a subsequent increase in the direct liabilities which have to be met out of parliamentary appropriations. The size of these is determined annually or bi-annually as the

There is no magic free money out of which the additional costs of this could be met. If there were no additional costs I would be glad to support, indeed to move, the amendment. As the Chair indicated, I would like to rule on the acceptability of the amendment, and I thank hon. members for assisting me. My first inclination was to accept the amendment and I have not changed my mind, although hon. members have indicated that the matter is not entirely clear. While we would want to be precise in following the procedural precedents and citations, I do not think members of the committee would want the Chairman of the committee of the whole to be unduly technical or precise, following the suggestion made one day by the hon. member for Peace River that the Chairman should not try to find sin where there may not be any. That is the sort of approach I would like to take.
The hon. member for Ottawa West raised a point of order which I am sure is not in dispute, namely, that if the amendment results in a direct charge on the treasury then of course it may not be moved by a private member. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, as I understand it, has argued that there may be an additional contribution to the superannuation fund by the employee and the employer, but that this would not involve any vote by Parliament.
While the matter is not free from doubt, it would seem to me that because there is not a direct charge involved, and because there is existing authority for this particular
vote, I should rule that the amendment is in order. Perhaps I should put it in a formal sense. It is moved by Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre):
That clause 27 of Bill C-207 be amended by inserting therein, immediately following line 16 on page 11, as a conclusion to sub-paragraph (ii) of paragraph (c) of subsection (1) of section 11 of the Public Service Superannuation Act, the following words:
"provided however that the reductions indicated in this subparagraph shall not be applied in the case of any employee who does not retire voluntarily from the Public Service;"

Mr. Chairman, I have a few observations to make on Part VII, clause 27 of this bill, but I shall limit my remarks to the first part of that clause, as has been agreed. However, I regret that Part VII is included in the bill at all because I see no necessity for including it as a consequence of any other part of the bill being approved by Parliament. I think it would have been much better had the government introduced Part VII of the bill as a separate bill, which could be referred to a standing committee of the House, where witnesses could be called, where people concerned and affected by the provisions of the bill could be heard, such as representatives of the Public Service Alliance, or anyone else concerned.
Even more important than the effect which this part of the bill will have directly on the people concerned is that the amendments proposed in it reflect or are characteristic of certain trends, trends which we as a Parliament have never carefully studied. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has stated that he is in favour of early retirements. That may be his point of view. I may hold that point of view or a different point of view, but I think that as a nation we have not decided what is an appropriate retirement age. There are trends toward younger and younger retirement. For example, the qualifying age for old age pensions has been lowered. The qualifying age for other pension schemes has been lowered.
I am not so sure that this is the best solution to the situation in which we find ourselves, because this is happening at a time when the lifespan of the general population, is lengthening and when generally speaking, statistically at least, people are remaining in better condition, both physically and mentally, to an older age. I think it can be argued that it is not in the national interest, or in the interests of the individuals concerned to put those people on the shelf, as it were, when they are still in good physical and mental condition and are willing and able to contribute to the productivity of the nation for a few more years.
There is also a trend at the present time to require more and more preparation to enter the labour force. A few years ago it was common for people to end their formal education and go to work at age 16, but now this usually happens when they are older because more training is required. Specialist professions such as medicine require many years of preparation, and I do not see why such a career is forcibly truncated by the notion that

March 30, 1971

everyone wants to retire as early as possible. I do not think that follows at all.
Of course, it will be argued that because of technological advances the production of goods and services requires less labour and therefore people must be retired earlier or there will not be enough jobs to go around. I doubt if this is true but if it is I think a better proposition would be shorter work weeks for a longer number of years in order to keep people productive and active as long as possible.
Early retirement means that people contribute to the pension fund for a shorter number of years and then, should they retire five years earlier than was previously considered normal, they will receive the pension for at least five years longer than would otherwise be the case. As a result, the rate of contribution must be higher in order to keep the fund actuarially sound. This makes it difficult to provide an adequate pension because, as we all know, a certain amount of inflation is inevitable. Apart from inflation brought on by artificial means or mismanagement, there is the inevitable rise in the cost of living. As populations increase the per capita quantity of goods and services to be distributed to them is reduced. This means that our material wealth must be obtained from more expensive sources. It is very difficult to provide an adequate pension if it is to be drawn for a great number of years, even with the cost of living increment provided by the legislation. It is almost certain that anyone who is on pension for a long time will die poor no matter how adequate the pension was at the start. If a person started to draw pension at age 55 and lived to be 90, which is quite common, I hate to think what the dollar would be worth then.
There is another important reason why this part of the bill should have been made a separate bill and have gone before committee. I think the civil servants affected by this legislation have a fundamental right to express their views before the committee. I recognize that the Public Service Alliance has made laudatory remarks about the bill. One of their statements reads:
The Public Service Alliance of Canada has welcomed the introduction of legislation that would permit early retirement without actuarial reduction of pensions for public employees in certain cases.
The major change is that an employee who has reached age 55 and has at least 30 years of service may retire voluntarily and receive an immediate annuity with no actuarial reduction because of early retirement.
I agree with that measure and approve that aspect of the bill because it has certain things to commend it which bring it somewhat in line with the age of retirement for persons in the military services, the mounted police and other categories who go on pension at age 55 or a little earlier, including members of Parliament in a few cases.
But that is not the whole story, Mr. Chairman. Like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I am concerned about the government's motives in the introduction of this bill. I should like to think they felt impelled to introduce it because of their interest in meeting the request of the Public Service Alliance but I am afraid I
Government Organization Act, 1970
am sceptical. I am doubtful if that was their only reason for introducing these amendments, especially the one which makes it possible for the government to forcibly retire certain categories of people on pension.
I do not know for what future possibility the government is providing, since they are not likely to reduce the total membership of the civil service. We all know that in the years of this government and its immediate predecessors the civil service has increased rapidly. More and more civil servants are being put into unproductive work which does not permit them to contribute to the national welfare as much as they might, but this is the result of government policy. Does the government intend to create a great number of vacancies in the civil service in order to allow that large group of people now in their early twenties to enter it? I do not know and none of these questions have been answered. I should like a much fuller explanation of the effect of this legislation on all categories of civil servants and of the government's intention on its application when it becomes law. How will it affect typical civil servants and how many will be affected? It is most unfair that people who have made a career of the civil service, who are reaching their most productive years when they can look forward to further rapid advancement from age 55 to 65, should be retired compulsorily. Promotional advances, coming at that age, would affect beneficially the pension of public servants. If for any reason the career of a public servant is terminated, prematurely or, at 55, say, the effect on the pension will be tremendously detrimental, because the six best years on which the pension is based would be years that would lie in the future of that civil servant. I, therefore, hope that the minister will give a fuller explanation of the purposes of this amendment to the Public Service Superannuation Act.

About a year ago some in the Public Service were laid off. The government reviewed the activities of departments and decided on the levels of staff which were fair and proper to enable the departments to carry out their work. Some members of the Public Service were retired at that time. I would not wish to suggest that there were very many. I think the total came to something over 400. A few of them would certainly have benefited if the provisions which are now before the committee had been enacted and on the statute books at that time.
These measures, in effect, provide more generous options for some public servants. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre put it very well. He said if you are 55 and have put in your full number of years of service, you may well welcome these provisions. On the other hand, if you have not reached that age and have not made your full contribution, then a certain number of difficulties arise. I think there is no member of this House who is not sympathetic towards the amendment which has been proposed, or towards the general purpose of the amendment. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says that if you are retired compulsorily there should be no diminution in the pension to which you are entitled. You take the number of years served, multiply by 2 per cent, and arrive at the result. I think all hon. members will need to reflect more on this point. The government is trying to put forward a principle, a principle of encouraging second careers. It wants to make the voluntary option of early retirement possible and to soften the conditions under which a number of people may be, have been or could be, shall we say, separated from their employment.
The problem is a serious one. If you are 55 and have served 35 years, there is no problem, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre put very well. Actually, a number of public servants have called me welcoming these provisions. The number of calls I have received welcoming these provisions is substantially in excess of those in which the caller has raised questions regarding any possible adverse application of these provisions.
If you adopt the principle under which you permit reduced pensions for those who are retired voluntarily, how will you square that with this amendment which says that if you are retired against your will, there is to be no diminution in your pension? If ever there was a provision which would encourage malingering, this would be it. In other words, if you were in the situation in which you could retire voluntarily, your pension would be reduced; but, on the other hand, if you made yourself obnoxious and were lax in the performance of your duty, and were retired, then your pension would not be reduced.

Mr. Chairman, in reply may I say that I have put nine years of my life into the Public Service and I have the greatest respect for the members of the Public Service of Canada who serve this country as well as any country in the world is served. We have a Public Service of which we can be infinitely proud. That does not alter the fact that the effect of the amendment will be to create the wrong types of incentives. There may be some people, and no doubt their number will be small, who might look on the matter in the way I have suggested. Our problem is that we must legislate without creating distortions and without bringing into play such motivation. The problem which hon. members of the House must face is, what is good public policy. I come back, Mr. Chairman, to the fundamental point.
The authority of the Government of Canada to retain or dispense with the services of any individual member of the Public Service does not hinge on the legislation which is before us today. This legislation softens the condition under which some employees, who might in any case have been retired, will be or may be retired. I think this will affect very few of them. Under these conditions, some pension benefits would be available to them. I would welcome a statement from the minister on this matter. I see he is in the House. I hope that he will make a statement to the House indicating that the government will maintain its role as a good employer, as it certainly has been, and that it intends to follow policies which will not be disadvantageous to any people in a technical way.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking to this amendment to clause 27 of the bill, I should like to take this opportunity to present a few ideas on superannuation for civil servants. It is convenient to give certain categories of civil servants the opportunity for early retirement, but in many instances this has to be agreed upon according to the nature of their jobs and special skills, which may diminish, rendering them less effective. There are however many features of this legislation that make it very suspicious. They could be used to serve other purposes.
I should like to point out that for those in the civil service who will be able to retire at 55, at a pension equivalent to 60 per cent of their salary, this provision is quite attractive. It certainly will be attractive to those civil servants who are over the $15,000 or $20,000 a year mark, in view of our very high rates of income tax at these levels. For instance, a $30,000 a year civil servant does not give up too much by taking early retirement, as the income tax branch is the main loser on this taxpayer. In fact, the $30,000 a year civil servant, or any other person for that matter in that bracket is only giving up about $4,000 and not the $10,000 that might be indicated. I should think there would be quite a wastage of the top level civil servants which the civil service can ill-afford to lose. Unless it is made attractive for these top level civil servants to remain in the public service, it would seem that the civil service will remain relatively scarce of expertise and the high training that many of these civil servants in the higher income brackets have.
Of course, we are approaching the time when the work ethic is diminishing in attractiveness to our general population. It certainly is true that many of the civil servants who will take advantage of this formula are in themselves very creative people. And from their point of view it will certainly be a great inducement to go into early retirement and enjoy those years between 55 and 65, when life can be more full for them in other lines of endeavour.
Then, there is provisions for retirement between 50 and 55 years of age as was ably stated in the House on February 2 by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. This poses some advantages and also some disadvantages. If a person is 50 or over but below 55 and had 20 years service, he would get approximately 20 per cent of his best six years in pension. This would be a very meagre return for him, particularly as many people in his category would be supporting fanrlies not yet away from home and not yet educated. If a $10,000 a year civil servant who is over 50 would only receive $2,000 in
Government Organization Act, 1970 pension he would find himself in an almost impossible position. He would have to look for other income and, being over 50 years of age, would find himself very limited in what he could procure in the way of jobs.
It is perhaps a tragedy that, as a result of the widespread inauguration of almost universal pension plans in our work force, older workers are just not wanted because of the pension requirements. Indeed, I am sure that a survey of small businesses would indicate there are many types of people working in these businesses who normally would be in larger companies if it were not for this pension requirement. Indeed, I would say that small businesses often depend on these people for their work force. I realize it is a very good thing for the individual to be able to retire at an early age and receive some benefits for his service and for his contribution. One of the attractions of the civil service has been that although the salaries have been considered relatively low in relation to private industry, perhaps it is not so true now, security of tenure and the prospect of a modest pension at the end of their career appeal to many people. For various reasons many people must change then-careers in mid-stream and it is a good thing that people who have to do this could receive a pension.
But, Mr. Chairman, there is another side to this problem in part seven of this bill in that the government may avail itself of this part seven and compulsorily retire people at age 55 on the pension they would get, or even down to age 50 on the reduced pensions provided by this legislation. If this is adhered to certainly there could be a great deal of unhappiness in the civil service. The hon. member who has just spoken said in no way provided for the severance of individuals from the civil service. One of the areas where it seems to me that this bill could be closely looked at is the retirement pension based on the average of his best six years. In the case of workers who have to retire between the ages of 50 and 60, or do retire, the resultant pension could mean a severe loss. The reason for this is that between the ages of 45 to 60 a civil servant, like most citizens, often receives rapid promotion and rapid increases in salary. At no time has this been more evident than at present, with the severe inflationary factor that has been prevalent in this past six to seven years. I think this formula could well be refined so that it would be based perhaps on the best year of his last six years or some such format that would give him a truer pension rate. This would be especially valuable when a civil servant has to retire compulsorily in order to comply with government regulations.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the advent and promotion of bilingualism in the civil service has created, is creating and will continue to create major upheavals in a normal career pattern. The advent of bilingualism in the civil service making it preferable that a civil servant be bilingual, and in certain cases mandatory, has added a large dimension and change in the job pattern. It is very obvious that many jobs that might be considered unilingual could be easily declared bilingual and necessitate a change of personnel. Furthermore, many people who are unilingual could never become bilingual, so it may well be that many civil servants will find themselves redun-

The now celebrated recommendation that $2 million is to be allocated for the introduction of 250 francophones, if we can define what a francophone is, indicates a fundamental change in the direction of the civil service. Although the government states that it is pursuing a policy of bilingualism, it is quite obvious that this must be set aside if the attempt by the government to equalize the number of those speaking French and those speaking English is to follow a mathematical formula. It is difficult to know what level the government would consider reasonable for the participation of French-speaking Canadians in the Public Service, but whatever it is that level should be defined.
There is no doubt about it, this policy will abrogate the merit system. If the government is to give up the merit system in exchange for some method of entry into the civil service other than by merit, we should know what this is. The $2 million program is almost certainly a make-work program because the special recruitment would apply to additional programs rather than complement existing ones and priority would be given to advancement of the 1972 program. None of these programs is in response to a public demand and at the moment even the government does not seem to know how these programs would develop.
The government has indicated that this is only part of a larger program to take into the public civil service some of our unemployed university graduates and presumably keep them from being drop-outs or other socially undesirable people. But government programs, once effected, have a great ability to carry on indefinitely and this is where I feel the Public Service Superannuation Act will come into effect. It will be a simple thing to cut the civil service in more prosperous times by lopping off those who will be in the upper age group and no doubt many of them will be unilingual and be unable to acquire bilingual status. Indeed, bilingual status may well be closed to them by means of administrative channels.
The development by the government of certain French speaking units only, which the President of the Treasury Board described as part of a policy to provide areas in which bilingual anglophones can exercise a proficiency in French, may well indicate that we are moving into an area of a dual language civil service. The mere fact that the Secretary of State is supervising the linguistic programs could well indicate that we are moving in this direction. In my opinion this might not be all that bad an idea, but if it is so, then it is obvious that this superannuation bill will be of paramount importance because it will be necessary to reconstruct the whole of the civil service and there would be much redundancy in many departments.
It is well known that the civil service is in a severe state of flux and the introduction of bilingualism has made it extremely difficult to apply the merit system on which the whole of the civil service has been based. But if we are to have wholesale changes within the civil service, and if a large number of civil servants have to leave the service prematurely, particularly in the age
group of 50 to 55, then it is most important that these people when they are compulsorily retired should get a fair deal. Much of the morale and security of the civil servant would be broken if after 20 years of service he were compulsorily retired on a salary less than he would receive as an old age pensioner on a guaranteed income supplement. Therefore, I do believe that it is most important to this House that it consider the retirement formula ought not be based on the average salary for six years, but perhaps on the salary of the best year of the last six.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak in support of this amendment. I am prompted to do so as a result of the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa West who raised the question of the government's right to fire or to lay off workers. This right was not brought into question at all, and I submit this is an attempt on the part of the hon. member to square himself. He knows that a number of members of the public service are alarmed about this feature of the bill, yet the hon. member says he intends to vote against the amendment. Therefore, he must find an excuse to justify his vote against it.
The hon. member talked about malingering and, in view of this, I think it is for us to suggest motives on the other side of the coin. Firings can be carried out for a variety of reasons which, although they may not be apparent, are thought or known to exist. At the present time there is too much suspicion, whether justified or not, that a lay-off immediately prior to pension, without provision for call-back, is done deliberately in order to save the government pension money. I think a lot of this suspicion is unjustified, but surely an amendment such as this would help to allay such suspicion.
Let me give the committee an example. think I should indicate what would happen on the other side of the coin. Malingering is a general term, something the hon. member would find difficult to prove. What is alleged to be malingering often is attributable to the incompetence of a minister or deputy minister who cannot run his department, with the result that the employees sit around with nothing to do. They are given no direction. Often this sort of thing is labelled malingering and the employees are blamed for it, rather than the blame being placed where it should be.
I think this amendment would remove once and for all any possibility of improper mot ve being attributed either to the government generally or to a minister or senior official with authority to hire and fire. If this amendment were adopted, then no one could say at a later date that an employee had been fired because the government wanted to save some money on his pension. Such suspicion would be completely removed. I should think that the President of the Treasury Board and the government-any government-would want to have this kind of provision so that when firings are carried out they are a direct result of government policy or some just cause on the part of the authorities, with no suspicion as to motive.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this particular amendment. First of all, I agree with the arguments that have been put forward. I will not repeat them because I know the government is anxious to proceed with the bill; suffice it to say that I think they are reasonable and responsible arguments. I find it difficult to understand why the government cannot accept the amendment, and for my part I intend to vote for it.
Having said that, may I take this opportunity to bring up a problem which is of special interest to my province and hence very local in nature. It concerns what is a consequence of this particular clause of the bill, an anomaly in the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada. Clause 2 of term 39 of the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada reads:
Canada will provide the pensions for such employees so that the employees will not be prejudiced, and the Government of the Province of Newfoundland will reimburse Canada for the pensions for, or at its option make to Canada contributions in
4746

March 30, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
respect of, the service of these employees with the Government of Newfoundland prior to the date of Union, but these payments or contributions will be such that the burden on the Government of the Province of Newfoundland in respect of pension rights acquired by reason of service in Newfoundland will not be increased by reason of the transfer.
That is section 2 of clause 39 of the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada, whereby Canada assumes the pension responsibility and the pay responsibility of certain public servants in Newfoundland who, pursuant to the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada, come under the federal civil service or under the jurisdiction of the Crown in the right of Canada.
The difficulty is that there are a number of federal public servants in the province of Newfoundland who, at the time of union, came under the jurisdiction of the government of Canada. Prior to union, these people were employed in the postal service, customs and immigration services and the Department of Finance in Newfoundland. Even though they may have reached the required age, they will not have the required amount of service by virtue of the fact Newfoundland has only been a province of Canada for 22 years. Consequently, they stand to be disadvantaged by this legislation. In other words, they will not be in a position to take advantage of this legislation. That is an anomaly. It is something over which they had no control at the time, and over which they have no control at the present time.
I feel that it is incumbent upon the government of Canada, having assumed the responsibility for these people under the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada, to live up to that obligation. More particularly, they should live up to the spirit of that obligation and make provisions whereby these people will not be disadvantaged or prejudiced in any way as a consequence of this bill now before the House. I say the spirit of the law as opposed to the letter of the law, because I am sure the President of the Privy Council and members of the government can argue on the basis of the letter of the law. They can argue on the basis of the precise wording of term 39 of the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada that this is legally the responsibility of Newfoundland and that the government of Newfoundland has to make up any deficiency to these pensioners.
I say to the minister if he were to apply that argument to the government of Newfoundland, I would point out that at the time of the signing of the terms of union this legislation was not anticipated. The situation was not anticipated whereby federal civil servants would be entitled to take certain retirement benefits at age 55. That is the crux of the problem.
I knew that the President of the Treasury Board is very interested in this because I have talked to him about it. At the present time, there are a number of cases before Treasury Board of individuals who are now pensionable and who are trying to acquire their rights. They are trying to establish their position as a consequence of that particular clause. I know that the minister is very interested in the plight of these people.
I put forward their case to the President of the Treasury Board, the government and the committee, with the
knowledge that the government will not hide behind the letter of the law, but will want to live up to the spirit of it. There are not many people involved. It would not be difficult to get a count of the number of people involved. There are certain employees of the postal department, the Department of National Revenue, customs officers, immigration officers, the Department of Finance and even certain employees of the minister's department, the Treasury Board.
These people expect to be justly treated by the government, not on the basis of some inadequacy of the terms of union. Rather than hiding behind the letter of the law, these people must be treated on the basis of the fact that they are now Canadians. At the time of union, the government assumed responsibility for these people. They became federal civil servants. They were not supposed to lose their rights of seniority and hence they should not lose their pension rights. I put this case to the minister. I hope that he will shed some light on it and give some words of encouragement so that these people will know what their rights are before the committee passes this particular clause of the bill.

There are no special provisions for all those people, none of the benefits which apply to those appointed by the Public Service Commission. It is to some degree to compensate for the lack of these advantages and benefits that this particular provision is being proposed.
While the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre indicates that this is a special benefit for a particular group, I would suggest that it is in some measure an amplification of the rule that there shall be relativity of benefits between various classes of employees. To some degree this establishes a more balanced treatment on separation between people with the status of deputy head and those appointed by the Public Service Commission.
I should point out that this is not a benefit unique to deputy heads. At the present time a number of employees in the public service are granted leave of absence without pay which means, as this proposed amendment indicates, that they are deemed to be continuing as public service employees although drawing their pay from other sources. This arrangement is made for people seconded from the public service to a number of international organizations. This is the arrangement made in respect of this number of public servants who become full time officers paid for by the various employee representative groups, unions, staff associations, etc. For these people, the arrangement is that they are on leave without pay. They are enabled to continue their participation in the superannuation plan by continuing to pay their own contribution as if they were continuing to be employed by the Public Service and by paying, as well, the government's contribution. Thus they pay the matching percentage and make a double payment. In other words, they pay double the normal percentage. It is this kind of arrangement for deputy heads which is being proposed here. It is the same kind of treatment that we allow for those who have been associated with the Public Service of Canada and have gone either temporarily or permanently to serve with international organizations or with employee representative organizations such as the unions. a (5:20 p.m.)
No one will deny, I think, that this is a benefit; but I point out that under an ordinary contributory plan the
Government Organization Act, 1970
employee through his earnings contributes one half of the cost of his pension and his employer contributes the other half. Those who describe the benefit derived by the employee who makes both halves of the contribution to the plan as a bonanza are overdrawing the picture a bit, I suggest. This is somewhat similar to the provisions of group insurance plans which allow ex-employees who benefited under a group insurance plan to continue to participate in the plan provided that they continue paying both their own premiums and the premiums paid formerly by the employer to the plan. That happens in a number of private plans in existence.
We hope here to make available to deputy heads or those with the status of deputy heads the equivalent of the assorted severance benefits which are available as a matter of right to those appointed by the Public Service Commission and, in so doing, make the government as an employer less heartless. It is hoped to make the government less heartless when, in the public interest, it becomes necessary to separate a man with the rank of deputy head before he has reached the full span of service or before he has reached the years of retirement. I hope, in order to establish some greater measure of fairness than now exists and to compensate to some degree for the lack of security of tenure of deputy heads and for the lack of the right to severance benefits of one sort or another which employees appointed by the Public Service Commission enjoy but which those appointed by other methods may not enjoy, that the House will agree to this particular amendment.

Mr. Chairman, it is not always easy to get an adequate reply in Parliament to a matter as important as pensions, but I cannot pass up this opportunity of raising two or three matters which have always bothered me concerning pensions in the public service. There is an anomaly in the service which I believe bears looking into. For instance, I do not suppose it is well known to members of this House that it was possible to serve in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police before the war, break your service in order to go overseas, come back to serve in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and then find that your pension rights were entirely different to those of others in the reverse situation. I refer to those who served in the armed forces, took a job at home during the war and then went back in the armed forces after the fighting was over. There is no uniformity.
I take the opportunity to raise this question because it is a personal matter. It has been cleaned up now. If this happened now and if we had a third world war, I understand that this type of service would be combined. But in most cases it is impossible to make these things retroactive. Fortunately, it only affects a few people. I have hesitated over the last 25 years to raise the subject because it is not liable to affect me, but this might be the last opportunity I have to raise it. Five or six- members find themselves in this bind. It is an obvious anomaly that a person who is in the service of the Queen should find himself penalized. Certainly it is not done on purpose, but through neglect in procedure the fine print of the regulations causes a person to suffer a very serious financial loss.
The second point I would like to make is that sometimes members of the armed forces and of the RCMP are asked to sign a contract with the government, giving in effect a blank cheque. In regard to widows' and orphans' benefits, members of these forces were asked to sign in good faith under different sections of the act which cover

their service, and in many cases they took a financial beating. One of the reasons they did so was that a smaller amount would be deducted from their pay at a time when their salaries were low, and they found it difficult to live on a small stipend; you could hardly call it a salary. They found it most difficult to get along, so they signed a paper to stop these deductions from their pay cheques. Unfortunately this affects a small but very important section of the population, widows and orphans of people who served in the RCMP and, in some cases, the armed forces. These people, not having read the small print and not realizing they were disenfranchising their widows and orphans, signed agreements which they did not understand.
As recently as this week I have written letters to some of these widows telling them that because their husbands signed away their widows rights some 25 years ago, they now have no recourse but to beg for war veterans allowance or go on welfare. I have begged the minister-I know he is very influential in the Treasury Board in all matters connected with this subject-to give this matter his attention and see whether there is not some way at this late date whereby people who have suffered in this regard can have their cases reconsidered. We find these anomalies in our pension schemes where men who have served exactly the same amount of time, and even hold the same rank, have a difference in their pensions of up to $200 or $300 a month.
While I am on this subject I would suggest that all pensioners in the public service should be entitled to a cost of living allowance. My own father, who rode across the plains on horseback in the old days when a mounted policeman received 50 cents a day, found himself at the age of 93 with a pension of $40 a month. The cost of living has increased considerably since 1893. Surely now we could very well, if we cannot make it retroactive, ensure that any pension schemes put in for the public service, for the armed forces or for the mounted police have a built-in cost of living allowance. I speak from personal experience when I say that one of the reasons we put up with disgracefully low wages in the mounted police and in the army was that we were told we would have security at the end of our service. If the cost of living is not taken into consideration, there is no security whatsoever. The attempts which have been made in recent years to increase pensions have not produced a magnificent effect.
I apologize to the House for having strayed from the wording of this bill but it is closely related to the rights of pensioners, particularly those who serve in the public service, and I wanted to bring the matter to the attention of the President of the Treasury Board.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Lamb-ton-Kent indicated that this is in the nature of a windfall for those holding the rank of deputy head or equivalent. He felt that they should be compared to people in private industry. This, of course, is partly the basis for the amendment proposed, namely, the kind of benefits which are available to those in senior executive positions in the private sector.
March 30, 1971

The hon. member cannot help but agree that what is provided here is indeed modest. We have found, in endeavours to recruit senior executives to the public service, that the kind of financial or economic advantages which are available to them are vastly more extensive and attractive in monetary terms than the government, acting on behalf of the taxpayers, can offer to attract this kind of talent to the public service. The right to participate or to continue to participate in a pension plan under arrangements which contemplate the employee or the ex-employee paying not only his share but also the employer's share of the pension plan does not seem to me to be going too far, in comparison with what is offered to senior executives in the private sector, nor does it seem to me to be in the nature of a windfall.
I think hon. members will be aware that there has been a desire by the government to achieve a greater degree of interchangeability of senior executives between the private sector and the public service than has been the case in the past. This prevents the public service from becoming too ingrown, too out of touch with what is happening outside the very large area of government activities, and at the same time it provides a bridge in the form of individual experience between the so-called private sector and the government sector. I think this is to be desired.
It is to be hoped that this kind of provision, modest as it is, will serve to enable one more effectively to carry on this kind of interchange that would be possible for public servants with ten or more years of service to move out of the public sector into the private sector. This would enable him, without too great a sacrifice, to carry on his contribution to the country. Correspond ngly, individuals who have had experience and who have talents which they have been exercising in the private sector would be able to move, perhaps not on a permanent but on a less than permanent basis, into the public sector, the government service, without, under the present arrangements, the virtual certainty that unless they continue for the rest of their careers in the public service no provision will be made in terms of pension or superannuation unless we have been able to conclude an agreement with prospective future private employers.
a (8:30 p.m.)
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has suggested that he would support a measure which provided that public servants who left the public service and went to work in the private sector could enjoy portability of pension. We already have agreements with a number of the provincial governments, but not with all of them yet, and with a number of corporations in the private sector, providing for the kind of portability which the hon. member has suggested and which I think is good and useful. But I am afraid it will be a long time before we are able, in a rather pedestrian fashion, to conclude agreements. The law requires that there be specific agreements-between the private pension funds and the public service superannuation operation covering transferability. I do not think it would be possible to reach this end on a general basis, given the vested rights
Government Organization Act, 1970
both of those who enjoy the benefits of this superannuation account and those who are the beneficiaries of and consequently have vested rights and interests in private pension funds. These must be the subject of individual agreements at present and cannot be legislated on a wholesale basis. Therefore I hope that the committee will agree to this clause.
In response to the hon. member for Pembina, I have the greatest sympathy with the lot of those of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who retired early a number of years ago. Under our system of contributory pensions, both the salary and the contributions which led to pensions of some 40 years or more ago were in an entirely different framework from those of today. However, we have operated these schemes on the basis that it is a contributory pension and, as a consequence of being contributory, the contributors have vested rights. These rights are precise; they are delineated, but they are also limited to the extent of the contributions made. While one could argue that, in social equity, those who in years gone by earned small salaries and consequently made relatively small contributions to pension schemes, and as a result drew relatively small pensions, are at a serious disadvantage nowadays and should be taken care of in some way, this is a problem which unfortunately is not unique with the public service but applies to a great many individuals in the private sector.
We have to try and cater to these needs as best we can through a series of, I hope, useful and progressive social measures, such as the guaranteed income supplement to the government's old age security scheme, the Canada Pension Plan and other similar measures.

speechtext:
It being shortly after the supper hour, Mr. Chairman, I very much doubt that I can reproduce the energy or the enthusiasm of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. Nevertheless, I wish to bring it to the attention of the committee that part IV gives birth to an entirely new breed of cat in the form of ministers and ministries of state. A minister of state is not responsible, like most other cabinet ministers, for a "line" department
Government Organization Act, 1970 but, rather, for a more narrowly defined area which, it would appear, will be largely associated with policy development or problem solving. A minister of state will have defined areas of responsibility, defined powers, duties and functions. These definitions will be contained in the proclamation establishing a ministry of state. In this respect a minister of state will be unlike a Minister without Portfolio who need have no specific duties assigned to him. In short, the proposal to establish ministries of state represents an innovation, a departure from established practice of an important kind.
I certainly have no objection in principle to departing from well-established practices of this House. Indeed, there are possibly many such departures which I would greet with exceeding great joy, even dancing in the streets. None the less, I think it only wise that such departures be agreed to only after the fullest study and the most complete explanation of the reasons which compel them. It is on this ground that I deplore the absence of the Prime Minister from the committee while we are discussing the portion of the bill before us, the portion of the bill with which he is most directly concerned, the portion of the bill which, if approved, will give him power to appoint at his own discretion up to five additional new ministers at the head of five new semi-departments and assign to each of them duties-an assignment which might well involve the major reorganization of existing government departments.
I repeat, the Prime Minister can do all this at his own discretion. I do not think that in these circumstances it is presumptuous of this House to expect the right hon. gentleman to be here to answer our questions. At least he should be prepared to tell us why he believes such a move to be necessary. At least he should be here to explain the use he intends to make of his new powers. At least he should be here to tell us what ministries of state he would anticipate creating, the sort of powers which would be assigned to them and the anticipated normal duration of such ministries.
Information of this kind is not available through a reading of the bill. The President of the Treasury Board who is here to answer for the Prime Minister cannot provide us with much of this necessary information because, in fact, the creation of ministries of state and ministers of state is, under this legislation, the prerogative of the Prime Minister and I very much doubt that the President of the Treasury Board includes among his numerous attainments the ability to read minds.
